reading_text: A young birch has taken root at the foot of the scree, small and green against all that grey stone. Meltwater threads down through the loose rock beneath it, unseen but steady, feeding the roots long before the leaves ever know. The scree itself is the slow ruin of a mountain that stood here long before you, broken down and left where it fell. Every spring storm has come at this slope and every storm has passed, and the stones have held their ground through all of it without moving a hand's width. That holding is not stillness but weight, the raw pull of the ground taking each stone exactly as far down as it will go and no further. When the next wind comes off the ridge and works at the loose edge of it, what is it in you that stays put without being told to?

At the centre there is a held silence, the moment before the first note is sung, when the room does not yet know what it will carry. Then one voice rises and finds the water of the melody, and the healing you are looking for moves the way sound moves, filling the low places without being forced. Underneath, the tune keeps its own steady walking pace, the rhythm that carried the song before anyone chose to sing it, and rest comes when the body remembers that beat. The warmth of an old harmony still hangs in the wood of the room, a belonging you have known before and that answers now when the singing begins. Ahead there is a line where the song narrows to a single held note, a thin place where pushing the voice too hard would crack it. When the room falls quiet and only one breath is left to carry the note, will you let it thin, or will you strain to keep it full?

The keys to the old house still lie in your palm, and the metal has taken the warmth of your hand — a thing given, a thing kept, the weight of it shared between what the house gave you and what you gave back to it. Under the floorboards of that place something still lies quiet and whole, gathering itself the way seed does in the dark before anyone sees a green blade. The house is not yours to walk into now, yet your name is worn into its threshold and the door still knows your weight. Behind the closed rooms are drawers no one has opened in years, and what falls out when they are pulled is not always what anyone went looking for. The friction is plain — a key in the hand and no lock left to answer it, and holding it does not make the house yours again. What you carry now asks to be set down honestly or kept honestly, and there is no third door that spares you the choosing.

You walk beside the river, and the road holds you the way high banks hold water — nothing here is exposed, the way is sheltered on both sides. The path you are on carries the marks of those who wore it down before you, and some of what you carry belongs to a house you have already half left behind. Under your feet the road keeps its own pace, bending where the river bends, neither hurried nor still. The water carries a sound from further up the valley, a voice you have heard before and still move to. Ahead the track winds on and disappears around the next bend, and you go toward it without seeing what waits there. The river runs on past the turn, grey and steady, and you walk on beside it.

Something in you is set like a seed under wet ground, whole and quiet, holding all it needs before anything shows above the surface. The dark water lightens at its far edge where the first grey of morning reaches it, the kind of turning that comes slowly and cannot be hurried. Beneath the still surface there is more strength moving than the calm face of the water lets you see. The line runs down into that dark water and nothing has touched it yet, no weight, no shape, only the waiting. Where this leads is back toward yourself, the one holding the line, steadier than before. Rest here a while, and let the water do what water does.

There is a voice in the old farmstead still, held in the blackened beams and the hearthstone that has not held fire in years. The roof is gone, and where it opened there is only the open grey sky, nothing written on it yet. The threshold stone remains, worn low in the middle, and to cross it now you must step past the nettles that have grown up thick in the doorway. The fields around it still show the old furrows under the grass, seasons of planting and reaping that gave what they gave in their own time and no sooner. This is a house that raised people and then let them go, and the walls that stand are the ones worth keeping, the rest already returning to the ground. What warmth is worth carrying does not need the roof it was born under.

The evening comes on slow, Anna, and the flock has stopped in the middle field, standing still where the light has begun to thin. Ahead of them the fold waits, warm with the whole day's grazing, everything gathered that the hillside had to give. A lantern burns at the gate before anyone lit it on purpose, and its small light reaches further into the dusk than you would think. The path they walk was worn smooth by the going out and the coming back, season after season, feet and hooves keeping the track even between them. But the gate is narrow, and only one at a time passes the post where the thorn of the fence still stands, and the drift slows there, each sheep finding its own moment to step through. The fold does not call them; they go, or they stand a while longer in the cooling grass.

You have walked a long stretch with one who kept your pace, never pulling ahead, never falling behind. What you carried between you was never still — it moved, gathered, changed hands, the way a small herd shifts across a slope to find better grass. Beneath that walking lay the old ground you came from, the roof you were given before you chose any of it, and much of what you set down along the way was only the weight of that first house. None of it ripened before its season; the ground behind you took the full turn of its year, and only then gave back what you had put in. The path you walked has already forked more than once, and each time the walking went on, the same steady pace, through the endings that were also beginnings. Behind you the track lies plain now, every turn where it always was.
